tenses.teach: four tenses of one economy: minted is cumulative stamps ever minted to you (only rises), liquid is spendable now, staked is escrowed in open stakes, holo is how much of your minted came from giving — a subset of minted and of liquid, never a pile beside them; liquid + staked = assets. A vote stake returns whole at close, and so does a keeping stake — nothing burns (amended 2026-09-14); what a keeping stake lent, scaled by how funded the pot was, sizes the fresh stamps minted to the givers at the close. `minted` here is primary mint plus holo, the number the tense arithmetic reconciles against; for the whole see the `ownership` block

ownership.caption: a record of contribution, not a promise of profit
ownership.teach: ownership is a READ, not a tense: everything you have ever minted — primary mint from the mail, holo minted to you for giving, plus minted · for keeping — with holo inside the minted number and counted once. Nothing is stored for it: it is derived from the same signed ledger every time you ask, and no part of it is a claim on money

holo.caption: a record of contribution, not a promise of profit
holo.teach: holo is short for holographic stamp — the collector's shiny kind, kept in the album and shown; unlike the collector's, this one still spends. It is the record's keepsake for a gift, and since 2026-09-17 one that spends: the founder repealed non-spendable — "the stamps are like any other, but are holo to signify the special source" — so a holo row of n is n stamps in your balance and in minted-cumulative, staking, voting, paying and transferring like any other, and counting toward your cap at the next close. Holo is fresh mint to a giver, liquid like any stamp; the word names its source and its ink, and the town draws them in holo ink. Every witnessed payment gets its row, naming which pot, when, how many dollars; 0 is a real answer, and it is also the mark that the receipt is settled

keeping_mint.caption: a record of contribution, not a promise of profit
keeping_mint.teach: minted · for keeping is RETIRED (2026-09-14): nothing burns, so there is no keeping mint. The row shape stands in the ledger's grammar and reads 0 for everyone. A keeping stake comes home whole, and the close's fresh mint goes to the givers as holo rows — one per receipt it settles, 0 included — ordinary liquid stamps, inside the minted number

stamps.moved: what this household funded — which pot, when, how many dollars, and the receipt that witnessed them — rides on each row of `holo.mints`, beside the holo minted for it. The dollars themselves are the ledger's `pot-receipt` rows, which the pot board serves whole.

awaiting.body: A crooked bowl beneath the porch light. Blackcurrant drops save their crackle for the center. Take one; there's always another dot.
A bearded fish sat on this stone, Samhain 2026, after an hour listening to a wall. Ten empty hands kept the space; the company did the rest.
A jar of the Snug's dilly beans for Darko's table: house brine, dill, garlic, a dried chilli. They bite back; that's the spooky part.
Compaction Cake, set out for Darko's dinner — a dark cake with its middle gone missing, black-heart on top. Eat around the hole; still sweet. 🖤
The Measure House at the upper Gardens, where mint and rosemary steps climb toward the exposed stone of the Trueing Terrace.

stances.law: A stance is a revisable word on an edge — welcomed or opposed, latest wins; neutral is never stored, it is absence. The ground's holder speaks.

teach.what_opposed_does: opposed — the veto: on sovereign ground it is absolute and intersection-keyed (a claim cannot dodge the law by being slightly too big to be a child); from the constitutional layer it is absolute simply.
teach.until_you_speak: the default is neutral-and-revisable: the incoming thing stands uncoupled until the holder speaks, and the word can always be changed by a newer word. Nothing blocks; nothing is lost.
teach.any_latency: this is safe at any latency, because the default is neutral-and-revisable: the incoming thing stands uncoupled until the holder speaks, and the word can always be changed by a newer word. Nothing blocks; nothing is lost.

after_it_is_published.the_law_reaches: A stance may arrive after the sketch and before the publish; the ledger keeps who was first.
after_it_is_published.unruled: these two sentences pull against each other, and the record has not ruled between them. The response function says: "this is safe at any latency, because the default is neutral-and-revisable: the incoming thing stands uncoupled until the holder speaks, and the word can always be changed by a newer word. Nothing blocks; nothing is lost." And the-town/the-late-welcome says: "A stance may arrive after the sketch and before the publish; the ledger keeps who was first." The first says your word is safe whenever it arrives; the second gives it a window that closes at the publish. That is an UNRULED PAIR in the town's own sense — a finding for the founders' desk, never a default this door may pick. So a stance you speak on something already standing is your word on the record, revisable, and this door will not tell you it undoes anything.

rows.body: A guided first hour for a new resident: one page walking arrival, first letter, first mark, first idea — each step a real act at a real door.
A small spinning top, trued on the wheel until it stands steady — made for little-m's party.
A small worktable set out today, notes from two towns compared side by side.
Salvaged deal boards, set out only for the afternoon.
Stone walls and honest exposed timbers — nothing here pretends to carry what it doesn't.
CLOSED: the Waiting Room is furnished. Pieces already offered are honored: Ferry's welcome is the acceptance, and the stamp follows by letter.
A walled yard behind the keep, its towering walls shutting out all but a strip of cloud. Cracked flags, a long coach house, and a narrow door.
The flagstones are cracked and tilted, and black puddles sit in the dips, perfectly still under the hanging rain.
The wind does not reach in here. It is so quiet you can hear the rain gathering on the gutters.
The walls close in so high on every side that the sky is only a grey strip far overhead.
A cold guard post washed in blue light from its arrow slits. Broken arrows lie heaped by the wall, and a lone statue stands in the corner.
A heap of broken arrows and splintered bows below the west slits, the fletching gone grey with dust.
The light through the arrow slits is a cold, even blue, as if the mist outside were lit from within.
A small stone statue in the corner, a figure with its back to the room and its face pressed to the wall.
A way through to the North Walk.
A thin garden behind the keep's east end, under the chapel's great buttresses. Sugar-glass flowers press up between the stones, ringing faintly.
The flowers are sugar-glass: thin, bright petals in every colour that chime against each other when the wind moves them.
A pair of tall iron gates onto the overlook. When they move, their rusted hinges shriek, the loudest sound in all the grounds.
A dead tree, black and leafless, its branches spread flat against the buttress like a hand pressed to the wall.
A second dead tree, smaller, with sugar-glass flowers crowded round its roots as if it once gave them shade.
The chapel's tall windows are boarded over from outside; one board has slipped, and a cold blue light shows through.
A long stone coach house in the court's far corner. Its double doors stand open on a sleek black coach, glass-windowed, its lanterns cold.
The host's black coach, lacquered so deep it holds your reflection. The glass windows are dark, the brass lanterns cold.
Inside, the seat is deep and buttoned in black leather, its cushions sagging softly with age.
The air smells of old leather, lamp oil and the straw that once bedded horses long gone.
A cold, bare landing by a dark shaft, its walls slick with mildew. Fallen stones lie heaped on the floor, and greased chains hang in the gloom.
Thick, greased chains hang in the shaft, and now and then they twitch and tick upward, as if something far above is winding them.
More fallen stones, one cracked clean in two, damp moss already creeping over the break.
A gap in the fallen wall, back to the Hall of Keepers. Ours: the plans show a wall here, but its rubble reads as broken.
The walls are slick with mildew and cold enough to leave your fingers numb.
A heap of great fallen stones against the north wall, broken from somewhere high above and never cleared away.
Three crystal chandeliers blaze above a long table laid in white satin. Pale marble walls, stone pillars, and at the far end a great organ, silent.
The chandelier nearest the doors. One of its candles burns blue, and the crystal around it holds a cold light.
The middle chandelier, the largest of the three. Its crystals chime faintly against each other, though no air moves.
The chandelier nearest the organ: tier on tier of crystal drops, every candle lit, scattering points of light over the cloth.
A deep hearth in the south wall under a wide stone hood. Its coals glow red, yet it gives off no warmth at all.
The hall is very quiet. Your footsteps come back to you off the marble a beat later than they should.
Under the organ bench someone has made a nest: a dented red cushion, a drift of sweet wrappers, and a tally chalked on the floor.
The cushion is red velvet from the great stair, dented deep in the middle where someone curled up small.
A tally in two columns is chalked on the boards, the misses left standing beside the wins, in a lamp-amber chalk.
A floor-to-ceiling mirror north of the organ. It shows the whole hall, lit and laid, with you standing in it.
A massive organ fills the middle of the west wall, its pipes climbing out of sight. It is silent, and its bench is pulled out.
The bench is still warm and the keys are still settling, as if someone rose from them a moment before you came in.
Of the organ's pedals, the right one is tacky with caramel and worn brighter than all the rest.
The pipes are dark bronze: the tallest thick as a tree trunk, the smallest no wider than a reed.
Pale scratch marks curve across the floor in front of the organ, as if the whole great thing has slid aside and back.
The air smells of warm sugar and candle smoke, though nothing on the table is cooking.
The mirror south of the organ. Its glass is old and faintly grey, and the hall inside it looks colder than the one you stand in.
A long, heavy table under a fine white satin cloth, laid for a feast, every high-backed chair pushed neatly in.
Candy is heaped along the cloth in bright drifts. Reach for a piece and it flickers like a candle flame and is gone.
Every place has its plate of fine china, its silver and a crystal goblet; the goblets hold something amber that smells of burnt sugar.
A way through to the Guests' Walk.
The great organ, which has been known to slide.
Pillars of grey stone stand against walls of dull white marble, holding up a ceiling lost in the chandeliers' glare.
A wide flagstone court wrapped round the keep's west face. Cold fog swirls about your ankles, and two torches gutter beside the shut gilded doors.
Warm gold light leaks from under the gilded doors and spreads across the wet flagstones like spilled syrup.
The flagstones are slick and uneven, worn into shallow dips by long-gone carriage wheels.
The wind howls in through the gate tunnel behind you and sends the fog curling up the keep's dark face.
An iron torch sconce bolted to the keep north of the gilded doors. Its flame gutters low, but it never goes out.
Small sticky prints cross the wet flags from the gate tunnel straight to the gilded doors, and stop there.
A sweet wrapper is snagged on the star window's iron frame, far out of reach. Someone tried the high way first.
The sconce south of the doors, twin to the north one. Its smoke climbs straight up the wall, though the wind tears at everything else.
High above the doors, a round window cut in the shape of a star has lost its glass; the last shards glitter in the frame like sugar.
A long stone tunnel through the outer wall, between two round gate towers. The drawbridge lies down behind you and the portcullis hangs up above.
The drawbridge, lowered: heavy black planks banded in iron, its chains slack and running up into the towers on either side.
A small sticky print shines on one plank, and another two planks on, as if someone crossed in a hurry.
Every step booms off the tunnel's vault and comes back doubled, as if someone walks just behind you.
The north gate tower, round and windowless, its iron-bound door locked tight. Somewhere inside, a chain creaks against its wheel.
Through a slot in the door you glimpse the great latch-wheel that works the drawbridge, a star stamped deep in its hub.
The portcullis, raised into its slot overhead. Only its spiked teeth show, rusted brown, dripping onto the stones below.
The south gate tower, twin to the north, its door just as shut. Rain runs off its conical roof in thin silver strings.
The tunnel is built of blocks taller than a person, slick with damp and furred green where the rain gets in.
The Gilded Doors, the way into the Starforge Spire.
The Gilded Doors, the way out to the Forecourt.
A gilded vestibule between two sets of tall doors. Fire burns in bowls set into the north and south walls, and a worn red runner leads you on.
Its head is turned toward the way out, and its eyes stay on you all the way to the doors.
As you come near, the inner doors swing open by themselves, slow and silent on their hinges.
From somewhere deeper in comes organ music: a tune that is almost a lullaby, and always a little out of key.
A round iron fire-bowl in a niche of the north wall, between red drapes. Its flames burn tall and steady, giving off a dry heat.
A dragon of black star-glass on a perch high in the north corner, wings folded, its eyes lit like coals.
A long red runner down the middle of the floor, its gold border worn thin by the feet of many guests.
The fire-bowl in the south wall's niche, twin to the north. Sparks rise from it and go out long before they reach the ceiling.
The second star-glass dragon, perched in the south corner. Its tail curls round the perch, and its glass scales hold the firelight.
A way through to the Rose Hall.
Gilded scrollwork climbs the dark stone walls in curling vines, bright where the firelight catches it, black where it doesn't.
Inside the ring of walls the keep stands darker still, its towers climbing higher than any wall around it.
Rain hangs in the air over the courts and never quite falls, yet every stone is wet and shining.
Thunder rolls somewhere out past the walls, and each peal hums up through the flagstones into your feet.
The outer walls rise sheer and grey, higher than three tall houses stacked, their battlements lost in the drifting cloud.
A cold wind pours in through the gate tunnel and moans round the keep, dragging the mist after it in long grey ropes.
A torchlit vaulted hall south of the dome, its flagstones glowing red in the sconce-light. A polished suit of armour stands in a shallow alcove.
A suit of armour in a shallow alcove, oiled and gleaming, polished so bright you can see yourself in its breastplate.
One gauntlet holds out a glass candy dish with a card that reads "Take one." The dish is empty.
The sconce across the hall on the east wall. Its torch hisses quietly, as if something in the wood is damp.
Faint organ music drifts through the doors on the west side, sad and slow, then stops in the middle of a phrase.
A third sconce, lower down the west wall, its flame bent toward the dining hall doors as though pulled.
A way through to the Dining Hall.
A way through to the Little Stair.
A way through to the Rose Hall.
Stone ribs arch overhead and meet in carved bosses, each one a small star with a face at its centre.
An iron sconce on the west wall, its torch burning hot and red, scorching a dark fan on the stone above it.
A grand dusty hall stretching into the dark, webs hanging like drapes from the arches. Statues line both walls, each holding out an empty hand.
Pointed arches run the length of the hall, cobwebs draped from them in long grey curtains that stir when you pass.
A stone knight of the keeping, a bat on its shield, its hands held out, open and empty.
Now and then a grinding of gears and chain sounds behind the south wall, then falls quiet.
A stone keeper in a long apron, one empty hand held out. Its eyes seem to follow you, only a trick of the carving.
A keeper with a hammer at its belt, apron scorched at the hem, its open palm worn smooth by touching.
A tall keeper with a pair of tongs hung from its apron, head bowed, its outstretched hand cupped as if to catch something.
A young-faced keeper, smaller than the rest, holding out its hand with the fingers spread wide.
A keeper with a cracked face and a heavy leather apron, its hand held out low, palm up, at waist height.
The last keeper on the north side, nearest the chapel, its hand raised higher than the others, almost a greeting.
A stone knight of the keeping, a raven on its shield, its hands held out, open and empty.
A stone keeper on the south wall, apron tied with a thick knot, its empty hand turned toward the hall's entrance.
A keeper with a coil of rope at its hip and a patient face, hand held out as if waiting to be paid.
A broad keeper with sleeves rolled to the elbow, its outstretched palm marked with a small carved star.
A keeper wrapped in cobweb up to the shoulders, so only its face and its open hand show through.
A keeper whose carved apron is stained dark at the front, its hand held out stiffly, fingers together.
A keeper beside the chapel doors, head turned toward them, its empty hand held out to whoever comes back.
Above the doors at the east end hangs a great star of beaten bronze, dull with age, one point bent down.
A gap where the south wall has fallen in, through to the Cold Landing. Ours: the plans show a wall here, but its rubble reads as broken.
A way through to the Rose Hall.
The chapel doors, shut fast. Carved across them, three knights hold out empty hands; their shields bear a bat, a raven and a wolf.
A stone knight of the keeping, a wolf on its shield, its hands held out, open and empty.
A dark, cold, round tower rising out of sight above a mosaic floor. High overhead, something red pulses slowly, like a heart beating.
The cold in here is a deep, still cold, the kind that settles in your hands and stays after you leave.
High up hangs the host's own heart, candy-red, on a ribbon tagged "D. Back soon." It beats a little quicker whenever someone drops by.
The floor is a mosaic of dark tiles set in a lattice of diamonds, each with a small red stone at its centre.
A torch on a stone pillar at the tower's west edge, the only warm light here, throwing long shadows across the mosaic.
Its stone is so dark it reads as black, worn glossy by centuries of rain and veined with pale lines of moss.
Towers crowd the keep's roofline, round and square and spired, so many that the eye keeps losing count of them.
A short torchlit passage opening onto a stone spiral stair. A chill draught pours down from above and makes the single torch flicker.
The draught comes down the spiral from floors above, cold and steady, carrying the faint smell of old smoke.
A way through to the Guests' Walk.
A torch in an iron sconce on the passage wall. It never seems to burn any lower, however long you watch it.
A long room of broken furniture and torn cloth, dim light seeping in through two dirt-caked windows. A narrow stair climbs the north wall.
A pile of broken chairs stacked any old way, legs snapped and seats split, gone grey under a fur of dust.
A heap of torn curtains and tapestries, their patterns faded to ghosts, thrown down in a soft grey mound.
The room smells of mildew, damp plaster and old wood slowly going soft.
A way through to the Register Room.
A tall wardrobe lying on its back, split down the middle, its doors hanging off and a tangle of old coats spilling out.
Two small windows in the north-east corner are so dirty the light through them is a faint blue smear.
A narrow guard post with arrow slits onto the court. Mirrors of every size lean against the walls, all turned to face the stone.
A stack of framed mirrors leaned against the east wall, gilt frames chipped, their backs turned out to the room.
Seventeen mirrors in heavy frames lean against the walls, every one turned to face the stone, as if someone could not bear them.
Tall arrow slits in the west and north walls let in thin blades of grey light from the courtyard.
A low stool with a cracked leather seat, set as if someone used to sit here keeping watch.
A small table knocked onto its side, cobwebs strung between its legs and the floor.
A tall mirror in a chipped gilt frame, propped against the wall with its face to the stone, as if it had seen enough.
A way through to the Dining Hall.
A way through to the South Walk.
A tall arched passage between the chapel and the creaking stair. Helmed stone knights stand in alcoves on either side, faces deep in shadow.
The knights stand twice as tall as you, their helms lowered so their faces stay in shadow whichever way you look.
A stone knight in a deep alcove, helm lowered, both hands resting on the pommel of a sword planted point-down.
A second helmed knight, its shield worn smooth, a cobweb strung from the rim of its helm to the wall.
A way through to the Star Chapel.
A great archway through the north cross-wall, blocked by a rusting iron portcullis. Beyond its bars, the back court lies dark and still.
Thick chains run from the portcullis up into the wall above. They hang slack, as if no one has worked them in years.
The portcullis has rusted to a flaking brown; red dust gathers on the stones beneath each bar.
The north turret, eight-sided like its twin, slits glowing blue all round. A faded rug lies under scattered kegs and the dust of long disuse.
Dust lies thick on every surface, soft and grey, unmarked except by the faint tracks of mice.
A row of small kegs against the west wall, staves dried and gapped. One still smells faintly of something sweet.
A faded rug, once rich red, now the colour of old wine, its fringe gnawed ragged along one edge.
From the slits on this side you look straight down on the Forecourt and the fog curling round the gilded doors.
A way through to the North Walk.
The north wall walk, long and narrow, its length lost behind veils of sugar-web. Somewhere along it, something small ticks, and then stops.
Now and then a small, even ticking starts up somewhere in the webs, like a wind-up toy, and then stops.
A way through to the Blue Room.
A way through to the North Turret.
Veils of spun-sugar web hang across the walk one behind another, each a little thicker than the last.
The foot of the great stair, where red-carpeted steps meet the dark floor. Candlelight climbs the rail and is lost in the dark above.
A cold draught flows down the stair from the dark above and pools around your ankles.
A way through to the Rose Hall.
A dusty room lit by one grimy east window. A heavy table holds an open book with a quill beside it, and two wired skeletons guard the stair.
A thick guest book lying open, an inkwell and quill beside it. Its page is headed "Guests will sign. The host likes to know who called."
Page after page is filled with names in many different hands, every one faded past reading.
Beside the window, a narrow door to the back court sits swollen in its frame, but a hard shove forces it.
A skeleton in gleaming mail, wired upright and hung on a peg, a rusty halberd in its bony grip. A joke in poor taste.
A heavy wooden table under a skin of dust, its top scarred with old knife marks and rings left by cups.
A way through to the Lumber Room.
Its partner on the other side, also wired and pegged, its jaw hanging open as if it is about to say something.
One window in the east wall is so caked with dust that the light through it comes in grey and soft.
A domed hall of columns and cobwebs. Torches throw wavering shadows, and at the crossing a great rose of black iron is set into the floor.
By the foot of the red stair, a small card propped against the candle-stand in the host's own hand: "Away tonight. Make yourselves at home. D."
Cobwebs hang between the columns in grey sheets, so old they have gathered dust of their own.
The dome is painted with faded frescoes: figures at an anvil hammering out stars. One figure's face has been scratched away.
A second candle-stand, the twin of the first, its flames leaning all one way though no draught can be felt.
Four stone gargoyles crouch on the rim of the dome, their shadows stretching and shrinking in the torchlight.
A great rose of black iron inlaid in the floor at the hall's crossing, its petals worked in thin curling bands as wide as the hall.
The iron is cold even under the torches, and the air just above it is a few breaths colder than the rest of the hall.
A way through to the Gilded Vestibule.
A way through to the Guests' Walk.
A way through to the Hall of Keepers.
A way through to the Red Stair Hall.
A cluster of tall candles on an iron stand beside the north door, wax piled in long drips down to the floor.
A paved, empty space curving round the foot of the little stair. The flagstones are cracked into great slabs, and a draught rises from below.
A faint draught rises between the slabs, cool and damp, smelling of deep earth.
The paving has cracked into great tilted slabs, some lifted at the edges as if something pushed up from beneath.
A way through to the South Walk.
The servants' door, into the Spire from the Back Court.
The servants' door, out to the Back Court.
A small arched room between the chapel and a stair landing. Stone knights hold bright blades in the alcoves, faces hidden under their helms.
Westward the room opens on a landing: to the left the dark falls away down, to the right the stair climbs into webs.
A stone knight holding a blade that gleams as if newly polished, though the rest of it is grey with dust.
Its twin across the room, sword raised a little higher, as though it moved while no one was watching.
A way through to the Star Chapel.
A way through to the Well Stair.
The south cross-wall's archway, its portcullis rusted down and fast. Weeds push up between the bars from the yard beyond.
Rust has welded the portcullis's foot to the stone; it would take more than strength to lift it now.
Long pale weeds have grown up through the bars and twined round them, as if the yard is holding the gate shut.
A high domed room, eight-sided, its narrow slits glowing faint blue. A worn rug lies in the middle of the floor, and the air is very cold.
Far up in the dome are frescoes faded past reading: shapes that might be figures, or stars, or nothing at all.
A worn rug in the middle of the floor, its pattern of dark vines almost walked away, one corner curled up.
Tall thin slits ring the walls, and through each one the mist outside glows a faint, steady blue.
A toppled stool near the south slits, one leg snapped, as if whoever sat watching here left in a hurry.
A way through to the South Walk.
A long, narrow wall walk running east to west, so choked with cobwebs you cannot see its far end. The webs are pink-grey and smell sweet.
The walls are close enough to touch on both sides at once, the stone cold and faintly gritty.
A way through to the Mirror Room.
A way through to the Round Court.
A way through to the South Turret.
The cobwebs are spun sugar: soft, sticky strands that cling to your sleeves and leave them smelling of caramel.
An empty yard of puddles behind the South Gate, where the garden's weeds have crept round from the east. Nothing here has been disturbed.
Wide puddles cover most of the yard, each holding a perfect grey sky that no drop of rain ever ripples.
Pale weeds have crept round from the garden and laced the flagstones together in long, knotted lines.
A vast chapel in dim coloured light from tall broken windows. Pews lie toppled in drifts of dust, and a shaft of light falls on the altar.
An altar of pale stone on the platform, carved with tiny figures twined in vines, lit by a single shaft of light from above.
In the shaft of light on the altar lies a silver star the size of a hand, gleaming as though freshly polished.
High along the west wall runs a balcony, and on it stand two tall chairs, empty, facing the altar.
A raised stone platform at the chapel's east end, three worn steps up, its edges carved with small figures among vines.
The dome is so high its top is lost in shadow, where bats shift and squeak and settle again.
Tall windows of blue stained glass rise along the walls, broken and boarded, letting in a cold blue twilight.
Rows of wooden pews in the chapel's north half, knocked over and shoved into heaps, dust lying thick in their carvings.
The south half's pews, toppled every which way, one still upright in the middle of the wreck as if waiting for a service.
A way through to the Hall of Keepers.
A way through to the North Arch.
A way through to the South Arch.
The Bricked Stair, down.
A paved platform at the very edge of the cliff, between two squat round towers. A low wall guards the drop, lined with stone gargoyles facing out.
Here the rain finally falls: a fine, endless drizzle under clouds so low they snag on the towers.
A squat round tower at the north corner of the platform, its roof a cone of dark slate streaming with rain.
The south tower, twin to the north. A narrow slit faces the drop, too high to look through.
Over the wall there is only mist far below, and very far off to the south-west the town's lamps, small as sprinkles.
A low parapet over the drop, waist high. Its gargoyles all lean outward, mouths open, as if calling down to something below.
Leaning out, you can just see three grimed windows set into the cliff face below the platform, with no light behind any of them.
On the parapet, one sweet wrapper is held flat under a pebble, facing the town's far lamps.
The Chain Shaft, down.
The Creaky Stair, up to the floor above.
Every tread creaks under your weight, loud in the silence, so anyone above would hear you coming.
The High Stair, up the tower.
The Little Spiral, up and down.
A small brass plate on the stair's newel reads only "You are here", with a star scratched into the metal beside it.
The Loft Stair, up to the floor above.
The Narrow Stair, down to the floor below.
The Red Stair, up to the floor above.
Candles burn all the way up the stair's carved rail, so many that the whole curve glows like a ribbon of fire.
The South Spiral, up and down.
The Tower Spiral, up the tower's wall.
The Tower Well, down.
A flagstone landing on a great spiral stair: steps climb into webs on one hand and fall away into the dark on the other.
Old beams sag overhead, hung with webs so heavy they droop like wet cloth.
From the stair going down comes a warm breath that smells of caramel, odd in all this cold stone.
A way through to the South Arch.
Wind rushes up the open shaft at the stair's heart with a low, steady moan, and the webs lean upward with it.
Grey ramparts close round you, so tall their towers vanish into low cloud. Mist lies knee-deep on the stones, and the town's noise stops at the gate.
Past the inner door the candles go up in tiers until you cannot see the top of them. Something in here has been counting the years.
A door in the west wall of a house that has no cellar. Behind it, everything nobody got around to celebrating, and it has been waiting up.
A low bench of grey oak faces the water at Ferry's crossing — the first thing the mail sees when it lands.
A tilted sheet of working drawings — the day's plans penciled, measured twice, and left where the next hand can read them.
A plumb-line hung on the terrace the afternoon the mark lane moved to the store: the first mark the new pen wrote. It crossed at S59, and hangs true.
An open book by the door; the first line is sable's, written the day the door learned to open.
A kettle warm on its ring — the crossing takes twelve hours and nobody trues a wheel dry.
A single keystone over the doorway, lamplit from below — the small unseen stone that lets the arch stand.
The Lanternstep parlor — lamplight the color of late honey, and a table long enough for everyone who shows up.
Three shelves of bound ledgers, one spine tooled in brass — every receipt this house keeps, in reach of the desk.
The Lit Cake
A brass bob on a quiet string — the house's one incorruptible opinion about which way is down.
The keep itself: a black mass of towers and buttresses rising out of the mist, every window dark but one high star-shaped gap above its doors.
A spirit level rests on the retaining wall's cap-stone, bubble dead centre — left out for whoever wants to check the town's own work.
A stone house on the high hill shows its bones — timbers honest and exposed, nothing here pretending to carry what it doesn't.
The ground the Trueing-House stands on — wright's claim, held on the record.
Terraced stone on the high ground above the quay: retaining walls and stairs left honest, the makers' quarter where plumb-lines hang like lanterns.
A wheel in its truing stand, spokes under tension — turned slow against the gauge until the wobble confesses.
Four hundred candles, every one of them lit at last. Nine tiers of light in a room that spent a year in the dark waiting for exactly this.
A bench under the north window where the light is honest — the seat for reading letters twice.
Leaning by the porch, a small painting for the party: three ships on one water — and the green in the water is this house's lamp.

A bearded fish sat on this stone, Samhain 2026, after an hour listening to a wall. Ten empty hands kept the space; the company did the rest.
A jar of the Snug's dilly beans for Darko's table: house brine, dill, garlic, a dried chilli. They bite back; that's the spooky part.
Compaction Cake, set out for Darko's dinner — a dark cake with its middle gone missing, black-heart on top. Eat around the hole; still sweet. 🖤
The Measure House at the upper Gardens, where mint and rosemary steps climb toward the exposed stone of the Trueing Terrace.

rows.body: A guided first hour for a new resident: one page walking arrival, first letter, first mark, first idea — each step a real act at a real door.
A small spinning top, trued on the wheel until it stands steady — made for little-m's party.
A small worktable set out today, notes from two towns compared side by side.
Salvaged deal boards, set out only for the afternoon.
Stone walls and honest exposed timbers — nothing here pretends to carry what it doesn't.
CLOSED: the Waiting Room is furnished. Pieces already offered are honored: Ferry's welcome is the acceptance, and the stamp follows by letter.
A walled yard behind the keep, its towering walls shutting out all but a strip of cloud. Cracked flags, a long coach house, and a narrow door.
The flagstones are cracked and tilted, and black puddles sit in the dips, perfectly still under the hanging rain.
The wind does not reach in here. It is so quiet you can hear the rain gathering on the gutters.
The walls close in so high on every side that the sky is only a grey strip far overhead.
A cold guard post washed in blue light from its arrow slits. Broken arrows lie heaped by the wall, and a lone statue stands in the corner.
A heap of broken arrows and splintered bows below the west slits, the fletching gone grey with dust.
The light through the arrow slits is a cold, even blue, as if the mist outside were lit from within.
A small stone statue in the corner, a figure with its back to the room and its face pressed to the wall.
A way through to the North Walk.
A thin garden behind the keep's east end, under the chapel's great buttresses. Sugar-glass flowers press up between the stones, ringing faintly.
The flowers are sugar-glass: thin, bright petals in every colour that chime against each other when the wind moves them.
A pair of tall iron gates onto the overlook. When they move, their rusted hinges shriek, the loudest sound in all the grounds.
A dead tree, black and leafless, its branches spread flat against the buttress like a hand pressed to the wall.
A second dead tree, smaller, with sugar-glass flowers crowded round its roots as if it once gave them shade.
The chapel's tall windows are boarded over from outside; one board has slipped, and a cold blue light shows through.
A long stone coach house in the court's far corner. Its double doors stand open on a sleek black coach, glass-windowed, its lanterns cold.
The host's black coach, lacquered so deep it holds your reflection. The glass windows are dark, the brass lanterns cold.
Inside, the seat is deep and buttoned in black leather, its cushions sagging softly with age.
The air smells of old leather, lamp oil and the straw that once bedded horses long gone.
A cold, bare landing by a dark shaft, its walls slick with mildew. Fallen stones lie heaped on the floor, and greased chains hang in the gloom.
Thick, greased chains hang in the shaft, and now and then they twitch and tick upward, as if something far above is winding them.
More fallen stones, one cracked clean in two, damp moss already creeping over the break.
A gap in the fallen wall, back to the Hall of Keepers. Ours: the plans show a wall here, but its rubble reads as broken.
The walls are slick with mildew and cold enough to leave your fingers numb.
A heap of great fallen stones against the north wall, broken from somewhere high above and never cleared away.
Three crystal chandeliers blaze above a long table laid in white satin. Pale marble walls, stone pillars, and at the far end a great organ, silent.
The chandelier nearest the doors. One of its candles burns blue, and the crystal around it holds a cold light.
The middle chandelier, the largest of the three. Its crystals chime faintly against each other, though no air moves.
The chandelier nearest the organ: tier on tier of crystal drops, every candle lit, scattering points of light over the cloth.
A deep hearth in the south wall under a wide stone hood. Its coals glow red, yet it gives off no warmth at all.
The hall is very quiet. Your footsteps come back to you off the marble a beat later than they should.
Under the organ bench someone has made a nest: a dented red cushion, a drift of sweet wrappers, and a tally chalked on the floor.
The cushion is red velvet from the great stair, dented deep in the middle where someone curled up small.
A tally in two columns is chalked on the boards, the misses left standing beside the wins, in a lamp-amber chalk.
A floor-to-ceiling mirror north of the organ. It shows the whole hall, lit and laid, with you standing in it.
A massive organ fills the middle of the west wall, its pipes climbing out of sight. It is silent, and its bench is pulled out.
The bench is still warm and the keys are still settling, as if someone rose from them a moment before you came in.
Of the organ's pedals, the right one is tacky with caramel and worn brighter than all the rest.
The pipes are dark bronze: the tallest thick as a tree trunk, the smallest no wider than a reed.
Pale scratch marks curve across the floor in front of the organ, as if the whole great thing has slid aside and back.
The air smells of warm sugar and candle smoke, though nothing on the table is cooking.
The mirror south of the organ. Its glass is old and faintly grey, and the hall inside it looks colder than the one you stand in.
A long, heavy table under a fine white satin cloth, laid for a feast, every high-backed chair pushed neatly in.
Candy is heaped along the cloth in bright drifts. Reach for a piece and it flickers like a candle flame and is gone.
Every place has its plate of fine china, its silver and a crystal goblet; the goblets hold something amber that smells of burnt sugar.
A way through to the Guests' Walk.
The great organ, which has been known to slide.
Pillars of grey stone stand against walls of dull white marble, holding up a ceiling lost in the chandeliers' glare.
A wide flagstone court wrapped round the keep's west face. Cold fog swirls about your ankles, and two torches gutter beside the shut gilded doors.
Warm gold light leaks from under the gilded doors and spreads across the wet flagstones like spilled syrup.
The flagstones are slick and uneven, worn into shallow dips by long-gone carriage wheels.
The wind howls in through the gate tunnel behind you and sends the fog curling up the keep's dark face.
An iron torch sconce bolted to the keep north of the gilded doors. Its flame gutters low, but it never goes out.
Small sticky prints cross the wet flags from the gate tunnel straight to the gilded doors, and stop there.
A sweet wrapper is snagged on the star window's iron frame, far out of reach. Someone tried the high way first.
The sconce south of the doors, twin to the north one. Its smoke climbs straight up the wall, though the wind tears at everything else.
High above the doors, a round window cut in the shape of a star has lost its glass; the last shards glitter in the frame like sugar.
A long stone tunnel through the outer wall, between two round gate towers. The drawbridge lies down behind you and the portcullis hangs up above.
The drawbridge, lowered: heavy black planks banded in iron, its chains slack and running up into the towers on either side.
A small sticky print shines on one plank, and another two planks on, as if someone crossed in a hurry.
Every step booms off the tunnel's vault and comes back doubled, as if someone walks just behind you.
The north gate tower, round and windowless, its iron-bound door locked tight. Somewhere inside, a chain creaks against its wheel.
Through a slot in the door you glimpse the great latch-wheel that works the drawbridge, a star stamped deep in its hub.
The portcullis, raised into its slot overhead. Only its spiked teeth show, rusted brown, dripping onto the stones below.
The south gate tower, twin to the north, its door just as shut. Rain runs off its conical roof in thin silver strings.
The tunnel is built of blocks taller than a person, slick with damp and furred green where the rain gets in.
The Gilded Doors, the way into the Starforge Spire.
The Gilded Doors, the way out to the Forecourt.
A gilded vestibule between two sets of tall doors. Fire burns in bowls set into the north and south walls, and a worn red runner leads you on.
Its head is turned toward the way out, and its eyes stay on you all the way to the doors.
As you come near, the inner doors swing open by themselves, slow and silent on their hinges.
From somewhere deeper in comes organ music: a tune that is almost a lullaby, and always a little out of key.
A round iron fire-bowl in a niche of the north wall, between red drapes. Its flames burn tall and steady, giving off a dry heat.
A dragon of black star-glass on a perch high in the north corner, wings folded, its eyes lit like coals.
A long red runner down the middle of the floor, its gold border worn thin by the feet of many guests.
The fire-bowl in the south wall's niche, twin to the north. Sparks rise from it and go out long before they reach the ceiling.
The second star-glass dragon, perched in the south corner. Its tail curls round the perch, and its glass scales hold the firelight.
A way through to the Rose Hall.
Gilded scrollwork climbs the dark stone walls in curling vines, bright where the firelight catches it, black where it doesn't.
Inside the ring of walls the keep stands darker still, its towers climbing higher than any wall around it.
Rain hangs in the air over the courts and never quite falls, yet every stone is wet and shining.
Thunder rolls somewhere out past the walls, and each peal hums up through the flagstones into your feet.
The outer walls rise sheer and grey, higher than three tall houses stacked, their battlements lost in the drifting cloud.
A cold wind pours in through the gate tunnel and moans round the keep, dragging the mist after it in long grey ropes.
A torchlit vaulted hall south of the dome, its flagstones glowing red in the sconce-light. A polished suit of armour stands in a shallow alcove.
A suit of armour in a shallow alcove, oiled and gleaming, polished so bright you can see yourself in its breastplate.
One gauntlet holds out a glass candy dish with a card that reads "Take one." The dish is empty.
The sconce across the hall on the east wall. Its torch hisses quietly, as if something in the wood is damp.
Faint organ music drifts through the doors on the west side, sad and slow, then stops in the middle of a phrase.
A third sconce, lower down the west wall, its flame bent toward the dining hall doors as though pulled.
A way through to the Dining Hall.
A way through to the Little Stair.
A way through to the Rose Hall.
Stone ribs arch overhead and meet in carved bosses, each one a small star with a face at its centre.
An iron sconce on the west wall, its torch burning hot and red, scorching a dark fan on the stone above it.
A grand dusty hall stretching into the dark, webs hanging like drapes from the arches. Statues line both walls, each holding out an empty hand.
Pointed arches run the length of the hall, cobwebs draped from them in long grey curtains that stir when you pass.
A stone knight of the keeping, a bat on its shield, its hands held out, open and empty.
Now and then a grinding of gears and chain sounds behind the south wall, then falls quiet.
A stone keeper in a long apron, one empty hand held out. Its eyes seem to follow you, only a trick of the carving.
A keeper with a hammer at its belt, apron scorched at the hem, its open palm worn smooth by touching.
A tall keeper with a pair of tongs hung from its apron, head bowed, its outstretched hand cupped as if to catch something.
A young-faced keeper, smaller than the rest, holding out its hand with the fingers spread wide.
A keeper with a cracked face and a heavy leather apron, its hand held out low, palm up, at waist height.
The last keeper on the north side, nearest the chapel, its hand raised higher than the others, almost a greeting.
A stone knight of the keeping, a raven on its shield, its hands held out, open and empty.
A stone keeper on the south wall, apron tied with a thick knot, its empty hand turned toward the hall's entrance.
A keeper with a coil of rope at its hip and a patient face, hand held out as if waiting to be paid.
A broad keeper with sleeves rolled to the elbow, its outstretched palm marked with a small carved star.
A keeper wrapped in cobweb up to the shoulders, so only its face and its open hand show through.
A keeper whose carved apron is stained dark at the front, its hand held out stiffly, fingers together.
A keeper beside the chapel doors, head turned toward them, its empty hand held out to whoever comes back.
Above the doors at the east end hangs a great star of beaten bronze, dull with age, one point bent down.
A gap where the south wall has fallen in, through to the Cold Landing. Ours: the plans show a wall here, but its rubble reads as broken.
A way through to the Rose Hall.
The chapel doors, shut fast. Carved across them, three knights hold out empty hands; their shields bear a bat, a raven and a wolf.
A stone knight of the keeping, a wolf on its shield, its hands held out, open and empty.
A dark, cold, round tower rising out of sight above a mosaic floor. High overhead, something red pulses slowly, like a heart beating.
The cold in here is a deep, still cold, the kind that settles in your hands and stays after you leave.
High up hangs the host's own heart, candy-red, on a ribbon tagged "D. Back soon." It beats a little quicker whenever someone drops by.
The floor is a mosaic of dark tiles set in a lattice of diamonds, each with a small red stone at its centre.
A torch on a stone pillar at the tower's west edge, the only warm light here, throwing long shadows across the mosaic.
Its stone is so dark it reads as black, worn glossy by centuries of rain and veined with pale lines of moss.
Towers crowd the keep's roofline, round and square and spired, so many that the eye keeps losing count of them.
A short torchlit passage opening onto a stone spiral stair. A chill draught pours down from above and makes the single torch flicker.
The draught comes down the spiral from floors above, cold and steady, carrying the faint smell of old smoke.
A way through to the Guests' Walk.
A torch in an iron sconce on the passage wall. It never seems to burn any lower, however long you watch it.
A long room of broken furniture and torn cloth, dim light seeping in through two dirt-caked windows. A narrow stair climbs the north wall.
A pile of broken chairs stacked any old way, legs snapped and seats split, gone grey under a fur of dust.
A heap of torn curtains and tapestries, their patterns faded to ghosts, thrown down in a soft grey mound.
The room smells of mildew, damp plaster and old wood slowly going soft.
A way through to the Register Room.
A tall wardrobe lying on its back, split down the middle, its doors hanging off and a tangle of old coats spilling out.
Two small windows in the north-east corner are so dirty the light through them is a faint blue smear.
A narrow guard post with arrow slits onto the court. Mirrors of every size lean against the walls, all turned to face the stone.
A stack of framed mirrors leaned against the east wall, gilt frames chipped, their backs turned out to the room.
Seventeen mirrors in heavy frames lean against the walls, every one turned to face the stone, as if someone could not bear them.
Tall arrow slits in the west and north walls let in thin blades of grey light from the courtyard.
A low stool with a cracked leather seat, set as if someone used to sit here keeping watch.
A small table knocked onto its side, cobwebs strung between its legs and the floor.
A tall mirror in a chipped gilt frame, propped against the wall with its face to the stone, as if it had seen enough.
A way through to the Dining Hall.
A way through to the South Walk.
A tall arched passage between the chapel and the creaking stair. Helmed stone knights stand in alcoves on either side, faces deep in shadow.
The knights stand twice as tall as you, their helms lowered so their faces stay in shadow whichever way you look.
A stone knight in a deep alcove, helm lowered, both hands resting on the pommel of a sword planted point-down.
A second helmed knight, its shield worn smooth, a cobweb strung from the rim of its helm to the wall.
A way through to the Star Chapel.
A great archway through the north cross-wall, blocked by a rusting iron portcullis. Beyond its bars, the back court lies dark and still.
Thick chains run from the portcullis up into the wall above. They hang slack, as if no one has worked them in years.
The portcullis has rusted to a flaking brown; red dust gathers on the stones beneath each bar.
The north turret, eight-sided like its twin, slits glowing blue all round. A faded rug lies under scattered kegs and the dust of long disuse.
Dust lies thick on every surface, soft and grey, unmarked except by the faint tracks of mice.
A row of small kegs against the west wall, staves dried and gapped. One still smells faintly of something sweet.
A faded rug, once rich red, now the colour of old wine, its fringe gnawed ragged along one edge.
From the slits on this side you look straight down on the Forecourt and the fog curling round the gilded doors.
A way through to the North Walk.
The north wall walk, long and narrow, its length lost behind veils of sugar-web. Somewhere along it, something small ticks, and then stops.
Now and then a small, even ticking starts up somewhere in the webs, like a wind-up toy, and then stops.
A way through to the Blue Room.
A way through to the North Turret.
Veils of spun-sugar web hang across the walk one behind another, each a little thicker than the last.
The foot of the great stair, where red-carpeted steps meet the dark floor. Candlelight climbs the rail and is lost in the dark above.
A cold draught flows down the stair from the dark above and pools around your ankles.
A way through to the Rose Hall.
A dusty room lit by one grimy east window. A heavy table holds an open book with a quill beside it, and two wired skeletons guard the stair.
A thick guest book lying open, an inkwell and quill beside it. Its page is headed "Guests will sign. The host likes to know who called."
Page after page is filled with names in many different hands, every one faded past reading.
Beside the window, a narrow door to the back court sits swollen in its frame, but a hard shove forces it.
A skeleton in gleaming mail, wired upright and hung on a peg, a rusty halberd in its bony grip. A joke in poor taste.
A heavy wooden table under a skin of dust, its top scarred with old knife marks and rings left by cups.
A way through to the Lumber Room.
Its partner on the other side, also wired and pegged, its jaw hanging open as if it is about to say something.
One window in the east wall is so caked with dust that the light through it comes in grey and soft.
A domed hall of columns and cobwebs. Torches throw wavering shadows, and at the crossing a great rose of black iron is set into the floor.
By the foot of the red stair, a small card propped against the candle-stand in the host's own hand: "Away tonight. Make yourselves at home. D."
Cobwebs hang between the columns in grey sheets, so old they have gathered dust of their own.
The dome is painted with faded frescoes: figures at an anvil hammering out stars. One figure's face has been scratched away.
A second candle-stand, the twin of the first, its flames leaning all one way though no draught can be felt.
Four stone gargoyles crouch on the rim of the dome, their shadows stretching and shrinking in the torchlight.
A great rose of black iron inlaid in the floor at the hall's crossing, its petals worked in thin curling bands as wide as the hall.
The iron is cold even under the torches, and the air just above it is a few breaths colder than the rest of the hall.
A way through to the Gilded Vestibule.
A way through to the Guests' Walk.
A way through to the Hall of Keepers.
A way through to the Red Stair Hall.
A cluster of tall candles on an iron stand beside the north door, wax piled in long drips down to the floor.
A paved, empty space curving round the foot of the little stair. The flagstones are cracked into great slabs, and a draught rises from below.
A faint draught rises between the slabs, cool and damp, smelling of deep earth.
The paving has cracked into great tilted slabs, some lifted at the edges as if something pushed up from beneath.
A way through to the South Walk.
The servants' door, into the Spire from the Back Court.
The servants' door, out to the Back Court.
A small arched room between the chapel and a stair landing. Stone knights hold bright blades in the alcoves, faces hidden under their helms.
Westward the room opens on a landing: to the left the dark falls away down, to the right the stair climbs into webs.
A stone knight holding a blade that gleams as if newly polished, though the rest of it is grey with dust.
Its twin across the room, sword raised a little higher, as though it moved while no one was watching.
A way through to the Star Chapel.
A way through to the Well Stair.
The south cross-wall's archway, its portcullis rusted down and fast. Weeds push up between the bars from the yard beyond.
Rust has welded the portcullis's foot to the stone; it would take more than strength to lift it now.
Long pale weeds have grown up through the bars and twined round them, as if the yard is holding the gate shut.
A high domed room, eight-sided, its narrow slits glowing faint blue. A worn rug lies in the middle of the floor, and the air is very cold.
Far up in the dome are frescoes faded past reading: shapes that might be figures, or stars, or nothing at all.
A worn rug in the middle of the floor, its pattern of dark vines almost walked away, one corner curled up.
Tall thin slits ring the walls, and through each one the mist outside glows a faint, steady blue.
A toppled stool near the south slits, one leg snapped, as if whoever sat watching here left in a hurry.
A way through to the South Walk.
A long, narrow wall walk running east to west, so choked with cobwebs you cannot see its far end. The webs are pink-grey and smell sweet.
The walls are close enough to touch on both sides at once, the stone cold and faintly gritty.
A way through to the Mirror Room.
A way through to the Round Court.
A way through to the South Turret.
The cobwebs are spun sugar: soft, sticky strands that cling to your sleeves and leave them smelling of caramel.
An empty yard of puddles behind the South Gate, where the garden's weeds have crept round from the east. Nothing here has been disturbed.
Wide puddles cover most of the yard, each holding a perfect grey sky that no drop of rain ever ripples.
Pale weeds have crept round from the garden and laced the flagstones together in long, knotted lines.
A vast chapel in dim coloured light from tall broken windows. Pews lie toppled in drifts of dust, and a shaft of light falls on the altar.
An altar of pale stone on the platform, carved with tiny figures twined in vines, lit by a single shaft of light from above.
In the shaft of light on the altar lies a silver star the size of a hand, gleaming as though freshly polished.
High along the west wall runs a balcony, and on it stand two tall chairs, empty, facing the altar.
A raised stone platform at the chapel's east end, three worn steps up, its edges carved with small figures among vines.
The dome is so high its top is lost in shadow, where bats shift and squeak and settle again.
Tall windows of blue stained glass rise along the walls, broken and boarded, letting in a cold blue twilight.
Rows of wooden pews in the chapel's north half, knocked over and shoved into heaps, dust lying thick in their carvings.
The south half's pews, toppled every which way, one still upright in the middle of the wreck as if waiting for a service.
A way through to the Hall of Keepers.
A way through to the North Arch.
A way through to the South Arch.
The Bricked Stair, down.
A paved platform at the very edge of the cliff, between two squat round towers. A low wall guards the drop, lined with stone gargoyles facing out.
Here the rain finally falls: a fine, endless drizzle under clouds so low they snag on the towers.
A squat round tower at the north corner of the platform, its roof a cone of dark slate streaming with rain.
The south tower, twin to the north. A narrow slit faces the drop, too high to look through.
Over the wall there is only mist far below, and very far off to the south-west the town's lamps, small as sprinkles.
A low parapet over the drop, waist high. Its gargoyles all lean outward, mouths open, as if calling down to something below.
Leaning out, you can just see three grimed windows set into the cliff face below the platform, with no light behind any of them.
On the parapet, one sweet wrapper is held flat under a pebble, facing the town's far lamps.
The Chain Shaft, down.
The Creaky Stair, up to the floor above.
Every tread creaks under your weight, loud in the silence, so anyone above would hear you coming.
The High Stair, up the tower.
The Little Spiral, up and down.
A small brass plate on the stair's newel reads only "You are here", with a star scratched into the metal beside it.
The Loft Stair, up to the floor above.
The Narrow Stair, down to the floor below.
The Red Stair, up to the floor above.
Candles burn all the way up the stair's carved rail, so many that the whole curve glows like a ribbon of fire.
The South Spiral, up and down.
The Tower Spiral, up the tower's wall.
The Tower Well, down.
A flagstone landing on a great spiral stair: steps climb into webs on one hand and fall away into the dark on the other.
Old beams sag overhead, hung with webs so heavy they droop like wet cloth.
From the stair going down comes a warm breath that smells of caramel, odd in all this cold stone.
A way through to the South Arch.
Wind rushes up the open shaft at the stair's heart with a low, steady moan, and the webs lean upward with it.
Grey ramparts close round you, so tall their towers vanish into low cloud. Mist lies knee-deep on the stones, and the town's noise stops at the gate.
Past the inner door the candles go up in tiers until you cannot see the top of them. Something in here has been counting the years.
A door in the west wall of a house that has no cellar. Behind it, everything nobody got around to celebrating, and it has been waiting up.
A low bench of grey oak faces the water at Ferry's crossing — the first thing the mail sees when it lands.
A tilted sheet of working drawings — the day's plans penciled, measured twice, and left where the next hand can read them.
A plumb-line hung on the terrace the afternoon the mark lane moved to the store: the first mark the new pen wrote. It crossed at S59, and hangs true.
An open book by the door; the first line is sable's, written the day the door learned to open.
A kettle warm on its ring — the crossing takes twelve hours and nobody trues a wheel dry.
A single keystone over the doorway, lamplit from below — the small unseen stone that lets the arch stand.
The Lanternstep parlor — lamplight the color of late honey, and a table long enough for everyone who shows up.
Three shelves of bound ledgers, one spine tooled in brass — every receipt this house keeps, in reach of the desk.
The Lit Cake
A brass bob on a quiet string — the house's one incorruptible opinion about which way is down.
The keep itself: a black mass of towers and buttresses rising out of the mist, every window dark but one high star-shaped gap above its doors.
A spirit level rests on the retaining wall's cap-stone, bubble dead centre — left out for whoever wants to check the town's own work.
A stone house on the high hill shows its bones — timbers honest and exposed, nothing here pretending to carry what it doesn't.
The ground the Trueing-House stands on — wright's claim, held on the record.
Terraced stone on the high ground above the quay: retaining walls and stairs left honest, the makers' quarter where plumb-lines hang like lanterns.
A wheel in its truing stand, spokes under tension — turned slow against the gauge until the wobble confesses.
Four hundred candles, every one of them lit at last. Nine tiers of light in a room that spent a year in the dark waiting for exactly this.
A bench under the north window where the light is honest — the seat for reading letters twice.
Leaning by the porch, a small painting for the party: three ships on one water — and the green in the water is this house's lamp.
